label: US policy and the preferences of elites and average citizens, 1981–2002

values.note: national survey questions on proposed policy changes, 1981–2002
narrow pro-change majorities got the change they wanted
majorities got the change they wanted even with 80% of the public in favor

citation: Gilens, M. & Page, B. I. (2014). Testing Theories of American Politics: Elites, Interest Groups, and Average Citizens. Perspectives on Politics 12(3), 564–581. Cambridge University Press, for the American Political Science Association.
caveat: Not a Hickel source; he cites it at TEA 12:13. The authors find that economic elites and business groups have substantial independent influence and average citizens little or none. Majorities who disagree with elites or organized interests 'generally lose', but citizens often get what they want when they agree with elites, and majorities opposing a change usually get their way. The authors conclude for 'economic-elite domination' and 'biased pluralism'; 'oligarchy' appears only in their summary of another scholar's theory. Elites are proxied by the 90th income percentile. Disputed: Bashir (2015, Research & Politics) argues the test understates average citizens' influence and that they won about as often as elites when the two disagreed; Branham, Soroka & Wlezien (2017, Political Science Quarterly) also challenge it. Gilens and Page rejected these critiques in a 2016 reply.
location: Cambridge Core full text: abstract; 'Majoritarian Electoral Democracy' (30%, 43%); 'American Democracy?' ('generally lose'). Critiques: Bashir's abstract and introduction read; Branham et al. checked via Crossref and a secondary summary only; the 2016 reply seen only in the opening of a reprint.

caveat: Not a Hickel source; he cites the index at TEA 13:10. An online poll of about 1,000 people per country, weighted by age, gender and education; average margin of error ±3.1 points. label: Welfare since the long 16th century: decline, then late progress

values.note: Europe, Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, China: incorporation into the capitalist world-system went with falling wages, shorter stature and more premature death
core regions of Northwest Europe
periphery and semi-periphery

citation: Sullivan, D. & Hickel, J. (2023). Capitalism and extreme poverty: A global analysis of real wages, human height, and mortality since the long 16th century. World Development 161, 106026.
caveat: Hickel dates the start of progress in the periphery to the early 20th century (TEA 1:10:04); the paper says the mid-20th century. Incorporation came at different times by region, not all in the 16th century (South Asia after 1757, for example). The indicators are proxies: wage records come from large institutions and may be unrepresentative, and the baskets cover limited goods. The authors note that many scholars whose data they use attribute these trends to population pressure rather than capitalism, and that further research is needed on what caused the later progress.
location: Open-access PDF: abstract; statement of conclusions at the end of section 1; 'Research approach' (data limitations); closing discussion (population pressure, limits of the baskets). Regional sections were searched, not read line by line.
